s: Duid is a younger brother (of the elder brother in the Taruma account)
q: Afterwards the younger brother Duid fished up the first woman

s: Duid marries first woman (after she is fished from a deep pool)
q: the younger brother Duid fished up the first woman from a deep pool and married her.

s: first woman produces fire (from her genital canal)
q: spreading her legs wide apart produced fire from her genital canal.

s: alligator takes fire (in its jaws)
q: an alligator came and snapped up the fire in its jaws and carried it off.

s: maroudi takes fire (by flying away with it)
q: Another day, soon afterwards, a maroudi picked up Duid’s fire and flew away with it.

s: Cora Indians identify iguana (as former possessor of fire)
q: The Cora Indians of Mexico tell how in former times the iguana, a species of lizard, was in possession of fire

s: man fetches fire (from the sky)
q: and fetched down fire.”

s: iguana is a lizard (species of lizard)
q: the iguana, a species of lizard

s: iguana retires to Heaven (taking the fire with him)
q: he retired to the sky, taking the fire with him

s: opossum steals a firebrand (towards the abyss)
q: the opossum seized a firebrand and dragged it towards the abyss

s: Sia Indians identify creator (as Spider)
q: The Sia Indians of New Mexico say that Spider was the creator of men and all animals.

s: creator is a Spider (creator of men and all animals)
q: Spider was the creator of men and all animals.

s: creator makes fire (by rubbing a sharp-pointed stone on a round flat stone)
q: there he made fire by rubbing a sharp-pointed stone on a round flat stone.

s: snake guards fire
q: setting a snake, a cougar, and a bear to guard the first, second, and third door

s: cougar guards fire
q: setting a snake, a cougar, and a bear to guard the first, second, and third door

s: Coyote carries cedar brand (tied to its tail and lit from Spider's fire)
q: Coyote hastened to the fire and lighted at it a cedar brand which was tied to his tail.

s: Navahoes lack fire (when men first emerged from the earth)
q: when men first emerged from the earth, they found the animals already in possession of fire, though they themselves had none.

s: Coyote passes fire (to bat when exhausted)
q: When he was exhausted, he passed the fire to the bat

s: sagebrush is used for fire-making by friction (bored with greasewood)
q: how to make fire by boring a hole in a piece of sagebrush with a piece of greasewood.

s: Karok Indians lack fire (in the early ages of the world)
q: The Karok Indians of California say that in the early ages of the world men were without fire.

s: two old hags guard fire (jealously, for the Creator)
q: For the Creator had hidden the fire and given it to two old hags to guard jealously.

s: ground-squirrel carries fire (as one of Coyote's animal runners)
q: Amongst the runners was the ground-squirrel, and the black spot which you see to this day just behind his fore-shoulders is the mark of the fire which burned him there when he was carrying it.

s: Sky God Obassi Osaw is a Sky God (in the Ekoi account)
q: the Sky God, Obassi Osaw, made everything

s: Thunder possesses fire (kept in his house)
q: of California relate how once Thunder carried off all the fire and kept it in his house

s: Thunder appoints Woswosim (to guard the fire)
q: setting Woswosim (a small bird) to guard it and to prevent people from stealing it.

s: Deer carries fire (in the hock of its leg)
q: But Deer carried some of it in the hock of his leg

s: Skunk kills Thunder (while Thunder pursues the fire thieves)
q: But Skunk shot him dead.

s: Nootkas tells such stories
q: Such stories are told, for example, by the Nootkas or Ahts

s: Sky God Obassi Osaw makes everything (at the beginning of the world)

s: Tsimshian are located in British Columbia (adjacent coastal tribe)
q: the tribes on the adjacent coast of British Columbia, such as the Awikenoq? and the Tsimshian

s: fire-making by friction extracts fire (by friction)
q: from which the Indians now extract it by friction.

s: origin of fire includes fire theft (as a recurring mythic pattern)
q: This arrangement of relays of animal runners,’ who pass the stolen fire from one to another, is a common feature in North American myths of the origin of fire

s: Thompson Indians inhabit interior of British Columbia
q: In a myth told by the Thompson Indians, who inhabit the interior of British Columbia, the Coyote reappears as the first thief of fire

s: Beaver conveys fire (in a clam-shell)
q: their version also the thief is the Beaver, and his accomplice is the Eagle, who diverts the attention of the owners of the fire, while Beaver conveys it away in a clam-shell.

s: Eagle diverts attention of Sky people (while Beaver steals the fire)
q: Eagle attracting the attention of the Sky people, while Beaver makes off with the fire

s: Eagle is assisted by Beaver (in stealing fire from the sky people)
q: Beaver and Eagle are deputed to secure the fire, and they do so as before

s: Raven steals fire (from the sole owner of fire in the Chilcotin Indians story)
q: But Raven contrived to steal fire from him by the familiar device of tying pitchwood shavings in his hair, dancing round the man’s fire, and then poking his head in the fire, so that the shavings ignited.

s: Raven is a fire-bringer (in Haida Indians tradition)
q: The Haida Indians of Queen Charlotte Islands say that long ago people had neither fire, nor daylight, nor fresh water, nor the olachen fish, all these good things being in the possession of a great chief or deity who lived where is now the Nasse River, and who kept them all to himself. But the cunning Raven contrived to steal all these boons from the selfish chief or deity and to communicate them to mankind.

s: Raven assumes form of spruce fir (as a leaf floating near the chief’s house)
q: but assuming the form of a leaf of the spruce fir he floated on the water near the house.

s: Raven possesses coat of feathers (which he could don and doff at will)
q: and donning his coat of feathers (for he could don and doff his plumage at will) he flew out of the smoke-hole, carrying fire with him and spreading it wherever he went.

s: Haida Indians inhabit Queen Charlotte Islands
q: The Haida Indians of Queen Charlotte Islands say that long ago people had neither fire, nor daylight, nor fresh water, nor the olachen fish

s: Tlingit Indians inhabit Alaska
q: The Tlingit Indians of Alaska also tell of the wonderful doings of Raven in the early days of the world.

s: Coyote is a first thief of fire (in a Thompson Indians myth)
q: the Coyote reappears as the first thief of fire, who stole it in the usual way

s: Raven has a bill half burnt off (when he came to land)
q: But so great was the distance that when he came to land the brand was almost consumed, and even Raven’s bill was half burnt off.

s: Tlingit Indians identify Snow-Owl (as guardian of the fire in another version)
q: But Raven (Yetl) knew that Snow-Owl, who lived far out in the ocean, guarded the fire.

s: wren has speckled plumage (because its feathers were burnt while bringing fire to earth)
q: But on the return journey all the wren’s feathers were burnt by the fire ; and to supply their place the other birds out of gratitude gave each a feather from his own plumage. Since that time the wren’s plumage has been speckled.

s: wren is respected in Normandy (because it brought fire to earth)
q: Hence in Normandy the wren is much respected, and people believe that some misfortune would befall him who should kill the bird.

s: theft of fire uses chain of animals (in American fire myths)
q: This story resembles the American fire-myths in which the stolen fire is said to have been passed on from one to another along a line of animal runners

s: Coyote steals fire (by dancing round a fire with a head-dress of combustible shavings)
q: the Coyote reappears as the first thief of fire, who stole it in the usual way by dancing round a fire with a head-dress of combustible shavings and then running away as soon as the shavings ignited.

s: Coyote passes fire to Fox (as part of a chain of animals)

q: the thief of fire is the Beaver, assisted by the Eagle or by the Eagle and the Weasel together.

s: Iphiclus recovers his virility

s: knife is stuck in wild pear-tree (by Phylacus)
q: Phylacus had pursued him with a knife because he saw him misbehaving; then not catching him up, Phylacus stuck the knife in a certain wild pear-tree

s: wild pear-tree contains knife (the knife used in Iphiclus's cure)
q: Phylacus stuck the knife in a certain wild pear-tree and the bark had grown round it
